steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a computer vision paper presenting SparseSwin, a Swin Transformer extended with a Sparse Transformer block that uses a limited number of latent tokens for image classification. Cover the shift from CNNs to vision transformers, the cost and parameter-count problems, our approach and headline results, contributions, and the paper outline.

steps.text:
- CNNs and large datasets in image classification
- Transformers and the Vision Transformer; their costs
- Efficient variants: Swin Transformer and SparseFormer
- Problem: large parameter counts
- Our approach: SparseSwin with the SparTa block
- Results, contributions, paper organization

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Computer vision is one of the critical topics in artificial intelligence. Most computer vision models use CNN as the method for image classification. To assess model performance, people use datasets like Imagenet because it has a lot of data and a variety of classes. Using large data when training the model improves performance a lot when it is tested on real-life or new data. Because CNN was used in so many image classification models, it evolved to a more sophisticated scale, connectivity, and forms of convolution.

But network topologies in Natural Language Processing (NLP) evolved differently, and now Transformer is the dominant architecture. The Transformer has even become dominant in computer vision, with the introduction of the Vision Transformer. The Vision Transformer changes the NLP transformer model so it can do image classification. Its architecture uses stacked Transformer Blocks to process image patches that do not overlap. Compared to CNN, Transformer-based models have large receptive fields and better performance on large datasets. Even though the performance is outstanding, excessive attention makes computing costs high, because the self-attention calculation depends on the input image size, and it also takes a long time to converge in training.

There is various state-of-the-art work that uses Transformers for image classification and improves the original Vision Transformer, making it more robust and efficient. One of them is the Swin Transformer. Swin Transformer uses local window-based attention so it does not use excessive attention on the whole image, and it reduces the computing cost of using a transformer on images. SparseFormer, on the other hand, adjusts the region of interest (RoI) by focusing on the front of the image with several latent tokens. This is done to extract features from the image. The advantage is that the calculation is only done on a limited number of tokens, so the self-attention calculation does not depend on the size of the input image, it depends on the size of the latent token, and this improves efficiency.

- Parameter counts
  - original ViT from NLP transformer -> 85M parameters
  - other work reduces to 27.6 M and 32M
  - still more than small CNN models with 12M and 26M
- Approach
  - inspired by Swin Transformer and SparseFormer
  - combine local window attention from Swin with limited latent tokens
  - Swin processes image in stages -> Sparse Transformer (SparTa) block compresses tokens -> classification layer
  - "Sparse" naming follows prior research
  - computation in SparTa depends on token size, smaller than input image
- Results
  - SparseSwin: 17.58M params vs 27.6M Swin-T, 85M ViT-B
  - fewer params plus better accuracy vs SOTA with identical params
  - 86.96% ImageNet100, 97.43% CIFAR10, 85.35% CIFAR100
- Contributions: 1. SparTa Block w/ limited latent tokens; 2. effect of regularization on attention weight in SparTa; 3. accuracy gains on ImageNet100, CIFAR10, CIFAR100; 4. smaller parameter size than SOTA Transformer
- Organization: 5 sections; 2 previous research; 3 approach; 4 experiments; 5 summary

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Computer vision is one of the critical topics in artificial intelligence. Most computer vision models use CNN as the method for image classification. To assess model performance, people use datasets like Imagenet because it has a lot of data and a variety of classes. Using large data when training the model improves performance a lot when it is tested on real-life or new data. Because CNN was used in so many image classification models, it evolved to a more sophisticated scale, connectivity, and forms of convolution.

But network topologies in Natural Language Processing (NLP) evolved differently, and now Transformer is the dominant architecture. The Transformer has even become dominant in computer vision, with the introduction of the Vision Transformer. The Vision Transformer changes the NLP transformer model so it can do image classification. Its architecture uses stacked Transformer Blocks to process image patches that do not overlap. Compared to CNN, Transformer-based models have large receptive fields and better performance on large datasets. Even though the performance is outstanding, excessive attention makes computing costs high, because the self-attention calculation depends on the input image size, and it also takes a long time to converge in training.

There is various state-of-the-art work that uses Transformers for image classification and improves the original Vision Transformer, making it more robust and efficient. One of them is the Swin Transformer. Swin Transformer uses local window-based attention so it does not use excessive attention on the whole image, and it reduces the computing cost of using a transformer on images. SparseFormer, on the other hand, adjusts the region of interest (RoI) by focusing on the front of the image with several latent tokens. This is done to extract features from the image. The advantage is that the calculation is only done on a limited number of tokens, so the self-attention calculation does not depend on the size of the input image, it depends on the size of the latent token, and this improves efficiency.

In previous state-of-the-art research, transformers for image classification have a problem with having a large number of parameters. For example, the original Vision Transformer takes a general transformer model that was used before in NLP and ends up with 85M parameter. Other research manages to reduce the parameters to 27.6 M and 32M, but that is still a lot compared to small and lightweight CNN-based models with 12M and 26M parameters.

We were inspired by the success of Swin Transformer and SparseFormer, so we combine local attention with the windowing technique from Swin Transformer and the use of a limited latent token to make it even more efficient. In our approach the Swin Transformer processes the image in several stages and then feeds it into a Sparse Transformer (SparTa) block, which compresses the amount of token and gives results that the classification layer can classify. This Transformer Block uses a limited number of tokens for its computation, so it makes sense to call it Sparse, like prior research did. The computation in the SparTa Block depends on the token size, so it is smaller compared to the input image.

The proposed SparseSwin model beat several other models in image classification. SparseSwin has fewer parameters, 17.58M, compared to the 27.6M parameter in the Swin-T model and 85M parameter in the ViT-B model. Along with the reduction in parameters, accuracy also improves compared to state-of-the-art research with identical parameters. SparseSwin got accuracies of 86.96%, 97.43%, and 85.35% on ImageNet100, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 respectively. Our contributions are:

- 1. We propose a Sparse Transformer (SparTa) Block architecture that uses limited latent tokens to improve the efficiency and performance of the Swin Transformer for image classification.

- 2. We looked at the effect of regularization on the attention weight we get in the SparTa Block.

- 3. We got accuracy improvements on the ImageNet100, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 benchmark datasets.

- 4. We got a smaller parameter size than the state-of-the-art Transformer model.

The paper has 5 sections. Section 2 gives an overview of relevant previous research. Section 3 describes our proposed approach. Section 4 shows the experimental results that assess how effective our model is. Section 5 summarizes our contributions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Computer vision has become one of the critical topics in artificial intelligence. Most computer vision models use CNN as the method for image classification [1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8]. To assess model performance, datasets such as Imagenet [9] are used because of their extensive data and variety of classes. Using large data in the training phase dramatically improves performance when the model is tested on real-life or new data. The use of CNN in many image classification models made CNN evolve toward a more sophisticated scale, connectivity, and forms of convolution [10].

However, network topologies in Natural Language Processing (NLP) have evolved along a different path, with the Transformer now the dominant architecture [11]. Transformer dominance has even reached computer vision with the introduction of the Vision Transformer [12], which modifies the NLP transformer model for image classification. The Vision Transformer architecture uses stacked Transformer Blocks to process non-overlapping image patches [13]. Compared to CNN, Transformer-based models have large receptive fields [14] and superior performance on large datasets [15]. Despite this outstanding performance, excessive attention leads to high computing costs, because the self-attention calculation depends on the input image size, and training takes a long time to converge.

Various state-of-the-art works use Transformers for image classification, enhancing the original Vision Transformer and making it more robust and efficient. One of them is the Swin Transformer, which avoids excessive attention over the whole image by using local window-based attention [15] and thereby reduces the computing cost of applying a transformer to images. SparseFormer [16], on the other hand, adjusts the region of interest (RoI) by focusing on the front of the image using several latent tokens in order to extract features from the image. The advantage of this approach is that the calculation is done on a limited number of tokens, so self-attention does not depend on the size of the input image but on the size of the latent token, which improves efficiency.

In previous state-of-the-art research, using a transformer for image classification suffers from a large number of parameters. For example, the original Vision Transformer adopts a general transformer model previously used in NLP, resulting in 85M parameter. While other research such as [15] [16] reduces the number of parameters to 27.6 M and 32M, this is still large compared with small, lightweight CNN-based models such as [8,3] with 12M and 26M parameters.

Inspired by the success of Swin Transformer [15] and SparseFormer [16], we combine local attention with the windowing technique of Swin Transformer and the use of a limited latent token to further improve efficiency. In our approach, the Swin Transformer processes the image in several stages and feeds it into a Sparse Transformer (SparTa) block, which compresses the amount of token and produces results that can be classified in the classification layer. Because this Transformer Block uses a limited number of tokens in its computation, it is reasonable to call it Sparse, following [16]. The computation performed in the SparTa Block depends on the token size, which is smaller than the input image.

The proposed SparseSwin model outperforms several other models in image classification. SparseSwin has fewer parameters, 17.58M, compared to the 27.6M parameter in the Swin-T model and the 85M parameter in the ViT-B model. This reduction in parameters is accompanied by an improvement in accuracy over state-of-the-art research with identical parameters. SparseSwin achieved accuracies of 86.96%, 97.43%, and 85.35% on the ImageNet100, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 datasets respectively. In summary, our contributions are:

- 1. We propose a Sparse Transformer (SparTa) Block architecture using limited latent tokens to improve the efficiency and performance of the Swin Transformer for image classification.

- 2. We examine the effect of regularization on the attention weight obtained in the SparTa Block.

- 3. We obtain accuracy improvements on the ImageNet100, CIFAR10, and CIFAR100 benchmark datasets.

- 4. We obtain a smaller parameter size than the state-of-the-art Transformer model.

The paper is divided into 5 sections: Section 2 gives an overview of relevant previous research. Section 3 outlines our proposed approach. Section 4 presents the experimental results assessing the effectiveness of our model. Section 5 summarizes our contributions.
